sentences.text: The known remains consist of disarticulated fossils from a single partially grown individual approximately 1.30 meters long.
Its teeth suggest an omnivorous diet, representing a transitional form between carnivorous theropods and herbivorous sauropodomorphs.
Panphagia possessed approximately 23 teeth that varied in shape depending on their position in the jaw.
The genus Panphagia was described in 2009.
Ricardo N. Martínez discovered Panphagia fossils in late 2006 in the Ischigualasto Formation of San Juan Province, Argentina.
Fossils of Panphagia were found in the La Peña Member of the Ischigualasto Formation within the Ischigualasto-Villa Unión Basin.
Panphagia fossils were russet-colored, embedded in greenish sandstone, and required several years to prepare and describe.
Panphagia's front teeth were recurved and sharp for eating meat, while the back teeth were vertical and spatulate, resembling those of herbivores.
The variation in tooth shape supports the theory that Panphagia was omnivorous, evolving from a carnivorous ancestor toward a herbivorous descendant.
Panphagia exhibits features similar to Eoraptor, such as hollow bones, sublanceolate teeth, and general body proportions.
Panphagia's skull resembles that of other basal saurischians like Eoraptor, and its lower jaw is more delicate.
Panphagia was described in 2009 by Ricardo N. Martínez and Oscar A. Alcober of the Museo de Ciencias Naturales in San Juan, Argentina.
Phylogenetic analysis identified Panphagia as the most basal known sauropodomorph dinosaur.
According to phylogenetic analysis, Panphagia is considered the oldest and most primitive sauropodomorph, displacing Saturnalia from that position.
Panphagia shares skeletal similarities with Saturnalia, including features of the ischium, astragalus, and scapular blade.
Panphagia lived during the early Carnian of the Late Triassic, evidenced by its association with a 231.4 million-year-old ash layer.
The time range for Panphagia is estimated between 237 and 227.3 million years ago.

Panphagia's presence in ancient strata suggests that the sauropodomorph clade separated from the saurischian common stem early in dinosaur history, possibly starting ten million years earlier in the Middle Triassic.
